content: 1. By 2021, all Member States were expected to complete and report baseline assessments of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in health care facilities. They were also required to establish national targets addressing sub-national disparities and implement national standards. 2. By 2023, all Member States were to integrate improved WASH services into plans, budgets, and implementation efforts aimed at enhancing care quality, strengthening infection prevention and control (IPC), combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and supporting universal health coverage. 3. Conducting a situation analysis and assessment is essential. This involves reviewing health and WASH policies, governance structures, and funding streams, alongside updated data on WASH coverage and compliance. These findings guide prioritization and resource mobilization. 4. National standards for WASH should align with the country’s context and serve as a foundation for designing, costing, implementing, and operating WASH services. Accountability mechanisms must ensure compliance with these standards across all facilities. 5. WASH indicators should be integrated into routine health care data collection and review processes. This data is critical for tracking progress and holding stakeholders accountable. 6. Community engagement is vital. Community members play a key role in defining, demanding, utilizing, and providing feedback on health services. 7. A roadmap for WASH improvements should be developed, supported by an intersectoral national team. This roadmap must clearly outline approaches, intervention areas, responsibilities, targets, and budgets over a defined timeline. 8. WASH infrastructure must be improved to meet national standards and supported by policies, resources, and strategies to ensure long-term functionality and service delivery. 9. Health care workers, including doctors, nurses, midwives, and cleaners, must have access to up-to-date WASH and IPC training during pre-service education and ongoing professional development. 10. Operational research and external reviews are necessary to test and scale innovative approaches, refine programmatic strategies, and share learnings. 11. WASH in health care facilities encompasses water supply, sanitation, health care waste management, hygiene, and environmental cleaning infrastructure and services across all facility areas. 12. The availability of WASH services, particularly in maternity and primary care settings, is critical for ensuring quality, equity, and dignity in health care. It also supports core universal health care goals and improves community health outcomes. 13. Unclean births contribute to over one million deaths annually, with infections accounting for 26% of neonatal deaths and 11% of maternal mortality. These issues are concentrated in lowand middle-income countries, where health care-associated infections (HCAIs) are twice as prevalent as in high-income countries. 14. Inadequate WASH services in health care facilities compromise safe childbirth and access to primary health care. For example, fewer than 30% of delivery rooms in some East African countries have access to water. 15. Hand hygiene is a cornerstone of infection prevention. Historical and modern evidence demonstrates its critical role in reducing maternal mortality and HCAIs. 16. Inadequate WASH in health care facilities contributes to the spread of antimicrobial-resistant infections, posing significant risks to patients and staff. Poor WASH also drives the prophylactic use of antibiotics, exacerbating AMR. 17. Unsafe disposal of health care waste, such as needles and syringes, increases the risk of injury, infection, and environmental contamination. Improved waste management can benefit both human and environmental health. 18. Many countries lack coherent WASH standards for health care facilities, and even where standards exist, implementation is often hindered by insufficient funding or interest. 19. Monitoring efforts for WASH in health care facilities have been inadequate. Reliable data on WASH quality, disaggregated by facility type and location, is essential for understanding needs and developing costed improvement plans. 20. Disease-specific budgeting often overlooks cross-cutting health system functions like WASH, leaving facilities underfunded for infrastructure investments, operations, and maintenance. 21. Health care staff are often overburdened and lack the training or incentives to improve and manage WASH services. Poor WASH infrastructure is frequently seen as an intractable issue requiring costly investments. 22. Most low-income countries and many areas within middle-income countries lack fully functioning municipal water and sanitation services. Addressing these gaps requires significant capital investments and intersectoral collaboration. 23. Since 2015, WHO, UNICEF, and partners have worked to improve WASH in health care facilities, embedding WASH standards in global health documents and advocating for practical steps at the national level. 24. Improved health care waste management, such as recycling plastics and converting organic waste to energy, can address neglected issues while benefiting human and environmental health.
